Practical solution (AREW) is elegantly simple, requiring only minimal modifications to standard policy gradients via advantage reweighting (Eq. 6)
Strong robustness analysis showing the method remains effective even with 50% critique noise, supporting practical applicability
Theoretical grounding via policy-gradient decomposition (Theorem 3.4) that formalizes the negative feedback loop between limited AS and BT
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, prompt templates, dataset descriptions, and training configurations in appendices
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem statement and informative visualizations that effectively communicate the failure mechanism
weaknesses: Limited theoretical guarantees: Theorem 3.4 only characterizes drift magnitudes within the locking regime without establishing exponential separation or formal proof that AREW escapes the regime

Limited baseline comparisons: no evaluation against other credit assignment methods, exploration bonuses, or the concurrent work (Zou et al., 2026) on reducing belief deviation
Missing ablations: unclear what happens with mismatched critiques (e.g., using AS critiques for BT) or alternative critique designs
Empirical proxies for AS/BT are task-specific, binary/discrete, and may not fully capture underlying phenomena; some improvements modest (FloDial-Easy: 3.7%)
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or number of random seeds reported

strengths: Identifies a clear and practically relevant failure mode (information self-locking) in outcome-based RL for interactive agents, with convincing empirical evidence (Observations 1-3 in Section 2.3)
Intuitive AS/BT decomposition provides useful lens for understanding coupled failures in active reasoning tasks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 tasks, 3 domains, multiple RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, GSPO), and two model families with ablations and robustness testing
Practical simplicity: AREW is lightweight (just advantage reweighting with binary labels) and easy to integrate into existing RL pipelines
Extensive implementation details in appendix including prompt templates and critique construction across datasets aids reproducibility
Consistent improvements over vanilla outcome-based RL across diverse settings, with some gains being substantial (up to 2-3x on some tasks)
weaknesses: Theorem 3.4 relies on unjustified strong assumptions (B.4-B.6) that are neither validated empirically nor defended theoretically: Assumption B.4 (self-destructive drift invariant to query choice) directly contradicts the premise that different queries elicit different information; Assumption B.5 appears circular (bounding progress by the quantity being improved)

Critical theory-practice gap: theoretical quantities (Ith, CBT) are defined using oracle Bayesian belief updates that don't exist for LLM agents, while practical proxies (e.g., non-domination in PE-G) are heuristic constructs with no justification for alignment with theory

AREW method is fundamentally hand-crafted and dataset-specific: critique construction rules differ across PE-G, PE-F, MediQ, and FloDial (Section C.3.1) with no principled design procedure for new domains; requires ground truth during training (e.g., comparing to w*) undermining applicability

Experimental evaluation lacks key comparisons: no baselines to intermediate reward shaping methods (CURIO, Sotopia-RL, SPA-RL) mentioned in related work, only compares to outcome-based RL variants; no statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals; unclear if improvements are significant

Proxy metrics for AS/BT are questionable: require ground truth during training, use dataset-specific heuristics, and lack clear correlation with task performance shown in Figures 2c/d where AS improvement doesn't always translate to reward improvement

Theorem 3.4 makes circular argument: defines 'weak belief tracking' as low CBT and proves agents with low CBT have low CBT; core coupling between AS and BT relies entirely on unvalidated assumptions rather than fundamental principle

Limited scope: all tasks have discrete actions/observations and short horizons (≤12 turns); unclear scalability to longer horizons, continuous actions, or open-ended reasoning; simulated interactive environments may not reflect real complexity

strengths: Novel problem identification: 'Information self-locking' is a well-motivated, practically relevant failure mode with clear formalization and intuitive AS/BT decomposition

Rigorous theoretical framework: Theorem 3.4 formally characterizes the self-locking regime with carefully stated assumptions; proves agents cannot escape without intervention; provides mechanistic understanding
Elegant practical solution: AREW uses simple advantage reweighting via binary directional critiques; theoretically justified (Prop. 4.1); minimal code changes; compatible with standard RL algorithms

Comprehensive experimental validation: 7 datasets across 3 domains, multiple RL algorithms and model families, consistent improvements (27/28 settings), robustness to critique noise, training dynamics analysis

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear writing with effective figures, extensive appendix with full proofs and implementation details, dataset specifications, prompt templates enabling reproduction
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theoretical analysis assumes oracle-belief MDPs and discrete state spaces, whereas LLMs operate with continuous representations; assumptions (e.g., B.4) may not hold in practice; limited empirical validation of theoretical assumptions

Critique design burden: Method is sensitive to directional critique accuracy; construction is domain-specific with inconsistent instantiations across datasets (C.3.1); limited guidance for new domains; requires ground truth or strong oracles

Hyperparameter sensitivity: Figure 5d shows significant sensitivity to reweighting strength λ_u with acknowledged 'non-trivial trade-off'; no principled tuning procedure provided; deferred to future work

Limited experimental scope: Mostly small, structured domains (PE-G/PE-F are toy problems); no comparison to alternative credit assignment methods or simpler baselines; unclear if SeL generalizes beyond active reasoning
Statistical rigor gaps: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; unclear if results aggregate multiple runs; makes reliability assessment difficult

Solution novelty: While problem identification is novel, the technical solution (advantage reweighting with auxiliary objectives) is relatively straightforward; limited conceptual novelty in the method itself

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Limited analysis of why agents develop SeL; what constitutes the 'non-interactive heuristics' learned; applicability to broader multi-step RL beyond active reasoning

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Information self-locking captures a genuine and previously under-studied failure mode in outcome-based RL for interactive reasoning, well-motivated through three concrete observations showing the bidirectional AS-BT coupling.

Rigorous theoretical framework: Theorem 3.4 and supporting results formally characterize the coupled learning bottleneck with capability indices, providing principled understanding of why SeL occurs (linear scaling of drift with I_AS and C_BT).

Comprehensive experimental validation: 9 tasks across 4 domains, multiple RL algorithms (PPO/GRPO/GSPO), and model families with consistent improvements (27/28 settings better than vanilla); thorough robustness studies show resilience to critique noise and structured perturbations.

Practical and simple solution: AREW requires only easy-to-implement advantage reweighting without calibrated rewards or separate models, making deployment feasible compared to dense reward alternatives.

Strong empirical analysis: Effective isolation of AS vs BT effects (Fig. 2c-d correlation analysis), demonstration of interaction-insensitivity in vanilla RL (MediQ intervention experiment), and detailed comparison with intermediate reward shaping showing robustness to critique chasing.
Excellent reproducibility: Extensive appendices with full implementation details, prompt templates, hyperparameters, and promised code release enable reproduction and extension.
weaknesses: Unvalidated theoretical assumptions: Theorem 3.4 relies on seven assumptions (C.4-C.10) stated formally but lacking empirical validation. Assumptions C.4 (action-invariant harmful drift) and C.5 (BT-capability-limited absorption) are particularly restrictive, and the paper provides no guidance on when they might be violated.

Critique construction oversimplification: Claims of 'easy-to-obtain' critiques are overstated. Construction methods (Appendix E.3.1) are highly task-specific, requiring domain knowledge (attribute trade-offs in PE, counterfactual consistency in MediQ). Limited guidance for practitioners designing critiques for new domains.

Weak belief tracking abstraction: LLMs lack explicit belief states; using confidence readouts Ψ_t as proxies makes strong assumptions about LLM internals. Assumption C.1 requires E[R|b_H] = f(Ψ(b_H)), but no evidence LLMs learn honest confidence under RL pressure.

Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares against direct intermediate reward shaping and vanilla RL. Missing: process reward models, step-wise verifiers, dense reward engineering, curriculum learning approaches, and empirical comparison with on-policy distillation (only conceptual distinction in A.1).

Restricted scope and generalization: All tasks are interactive reasoning — no evidence SeL applies to non-interactive long-horizon RL. Many tasks synthetic (PE-G/PE-F designed for information seeking). Tau2Bench evaluation minimal (2 settings with different model sizes).

Insufficient statistical rigor: Main results (Table 1) lack error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. No specification of single vs multiple runs. Some improvements (e.g., 3-7 points on FloDial-Easy) may be within noise margins.

Oracle-belief circularity: Oracle-good actions (Def. C.19) and weighted accuracy in Prop. 4.1 require knowing terminal oracle confidence, but in practice z_t is constructed without this. Gap between theoretical guarantees and practical applicability.

Incomplete failure analysis: No systematic study of when AREW fails, when critique quality is very poor (α > 0.5), or whether AS-BT decomposition applies universally. Edge cases and negative results absent.

Clever proxy design enabling fine-grained analysis of coupled failures between action selection and belief tracking
Extensive empirical evaluation across 9 tasks with robustness analyses and multiple RL algorithms
Simple, practical AREW method that preserves task rewards without requiring learned reward models
Comprehensive supplementary materials with detailed proofs and implementation details
weaknesses: Theoretical contribution is incremental—Theorem 3.4 relies on 7 restrictive assumptions and shows expected behavior (low-capability systems improve slowly); significant theory-practice gap between oracle Bayesian beliefs and learned LLM policies

Critical task-specific engineering undermines generalizability—directional critiques require extensive customization for each domain (PE, MediQ, FloDial, Tau2-Bench), contradicting claims of lightweight applicability

Empirical proxy definitions (task-specific notions of informativeness and belief quality) may be biased to favor AREW; insufficient baseline comparisons with process rewards or hierarchical RL methods

AREW method has practical limitations: Proposition 4.1 shows effectiveness depends on high weighted accuracy (>0.5) with linear improvement scaling; hyperparameter λu is sensitive with no principled selection method

Presentation is dense with poor narrative flow—Section 3 theory feels disconnected from practical problems; notation-heavy with main results lacking clarity; Theorem 3.4 informal version omits key assumptions

Generalization concerns—all tasks are interactive reasoning with ground truth; unclear if SeL occurs beyond this domain; model scale limited to 7B-14B; open-ended reasoning and multi-task scenarios unexplored
Causality claims weakly supported—Observation 2 uses counterfactual interventions on oracle models rather than causal analysis of actual learning dynamics

strengths: Novel problem identification: Information Self-Locking is a compelling and practically important failure mode, well-motivated through careful empirical observations showing rewards improve while information-seeking deteriorates
Clear conceptual framework: The AS-BT decomposition provides excellent analytical leverage for understanding the bidirectional coupling that traps agents in low-information regimes

Solid theoretical contribution: Formal definitions (IAS, CBT), the locking regime formulation, and Theorem 3.4 rigorously characterize learning dynamics; Proposition 4.1 elegantly relates AREW effectiveness to weighted accuracy

Comprehensive experimental validation: 9 tasks across 4 domains with multiple RL algorithms and model families; consistent improvements and extensive robustness analysis (noise, perturbations, hyperparameter sensitivity)
Practical solution: AREW is lightweight, requires only binary directional critiques rather than calibrated rewards or learned models, integrates easily with standard RL pipelines
Methodological rigor: Task-grounded proxies validated via rubric-based evaluation; controlled experiments isolating specific phenomena; extended comparisons with reward shaping baselines
Excellent presentation: Clear motivation, effective examples, rigorous proofs in appendix, comprehensive implementation details
weaknesses: Gap between theory and practice: Theoretical framework assumes explicit belief states b_t ∈ Δ(S) while LLM agents don't maintain such representations; regularity assumptions (C.4-C.10) are strong and their necessity for non-convex LLM training unclear; first-order analysis fragility unaddressed

Critique construction generalization: Despite 'easy-to-obtain' framing, actual construction is task-specific and non-trivial (trade-off detection, counterfactual consistency, invariance rules); no principled framework for novel domains; requires access to ground truth s⋆ in some cases

Limited baseline comparisons: No comparison with other structured credit assignment methods (process reward models, CURIO, SPA-RL, or methods optimizing information gain); intermediate reward comparison only on 2 datasets

Experimental scope: All tasks have clear ground truth and well-defined correctness; structured domains (multiple-choice, comparisons); small-to-medium models only (7B-14B); scaling to frontier models unexplored; sensitivity to horizon length unstudied

Hyperparameter sensitivity: Figure 9b shows strong sensitivity to λ with limited guidance; binary critique choice appears arbitrary without ablation; likelihood-margin objective motivation post-hoc with no alternative design exploration

Theoretical gaps: Proposition 4.1 assumes diagonal score-covariance without full justification; no convergence rate or sample complexity analysis; connection between Thm. 3.4 (problem characterization) and AREW design not rigorously established

Reproducibility and design choices: Code URL not provided; some implementation details scattered; hyperparameter choices incomplete; τ²-bench uses GPT-4o simulation rather than real interactions; statistical significance tests absent
